title: An RKE2 cluster boots from nothing
subtitle: One binary, a systemd unit, and a bootstrap that pulls itself up
scenario:
Three fresh VMs and a load balancer. No Kubernetes anywhere, no kubectl, nothing running.

By the end of this you will have a three-server HA control plane and a worker — and you will know which file to touch when any of it misbehaves.

steps.title: The load balancer comes first

ask.prompt: Why set up the fixed registration address before installing the first server, rather than after?
choices: So every certificate is issued containing that name from the start — adding it later means rotating certs
Because RKE2 refuses to start without a load balancer
So etcd can elect a leader across all three nodes at once
It makes no difference; the address is only used at install time
ask.explain: The API server certificate only contains the names it was issued with. Point kubectl at an address that is not in `tls-san` and TLS fails on the name. Retrofitting it means stopping the service, deleting the serving certs and restarting — easy to get right on day one, annoying on day 200.

steps.body:
Pick a name that will front all three servers — a load balancer VIP or a DNS record — and decide it now: `k8s-prod.internal`.

Every node will register through it, and every certificate will contain it. Pointing all your nodes at `server-1` instead is the mistake that turns one machine into a permanent single point of failure for joins and re-registration.

code.label: what the LB needs to carry
code.text:
6443/tcp   Kubernetes API      -> all three servers
9345/tcp   RKE2 supervisor     -> all three servers   (node registration)

node-to-node, not through the LB:
2379-2380  etcd client + peer  servers <-> servers
10250/tcp  kubelet API         servers -> all nodes
8472/udp   Flannel VXLAN       all <-> all

steps.watch: A firewall that allows 6443 but not 9345 gives you a cluster where kubectl works perfectly and no new node can ever join.

steps.title: Configuration before installation
steps.body:
RKE2 reads `/etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml` at startup and renders everything else from it: kubelet config, containerd config, and the control-plane static pod manifests.

Write it before you start the service. Some of these can only be set at bootstrap — `cni` in particular cannot be changed later.

The `token` is a cluster-level secret. Anyone holding it can register a node into your cluster, so it belongs in your secrets manager, not in the repo.

code.label: /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml on the first server
code.text:
token: <shared-secret>
tls-san:
  - k8s-prod.internal
  - 10.0.0.100
cni: canal
profile: cis
disable:
  - rke2-ingress-nginx        # we run our own
etcd-snapshot-schedule-cron: "0 */6 * * *"
etcd-snapshot-retention: 20
kube-apiserver-arg:
  - "audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log"
code.note: No `server:` key on the first server. That absence is what makes it the one that initializes the cluster.

steps.title: systemctl start, and the bootstrap paradox

ask.prompt: There is no API server running yet, so how does the kube-apiserver container get started?
choices: RKE2's kubelet reads static pod manifests off local disk and starts them with no API server involved
rke2-server runs the API server as a goroutine inside its own process
A bootstrap Deployment is applied from an embedded manifest
containerd is configured to auto-start it at boot
ask.explain: This is the trick that resolves the chicken-and-egg. The kubelet can run pods from files on disk — no API needed. It starts etcd and the API server that way, and only then can anything else talk to Kubernetes at all.

steps.body:
`systemctl start rke2-server` unpacks the binaries, starts RKE2's **own bundled containerd**, generates the certificate authorities, and starts a kubelet.

That kubelet is pointed at a directory of **static pod** manifests. It reads the files and starts etcd, kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager as containers — with nothing to ask for permission from.

Once the API server is up, those static pods appear in `kubectl` as read-only **mirror pods**. Deleting one via kubectl just bounces it; the file on disk is the source of truth.

code.label: the control plane, as files
code.text:
$ ls /var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/pod-manifests/
etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml

$ export PATH=$PATH:/var/lib/rancher/rke2/bin
$ export KUBECONFIG=/etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml
$ kubectl get pod -n kube-system kube-apiserver-server-1 \
    -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind}'
Node
code.note: Owned by a Node, not a Deployment. That is the signature of a static pod.

steps.watch: Put those two export lines in root's .bashrc on every server. They are the first thing you need in an incident.

steps.title: The cluster installs its own add-ons
steps.body:
RKE2 drops YAML into `/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests/` and applies anything it finds there at startup. Most of it is `HelmChart` custom resources.

A built-in **helm-controller** watches those and, for each one, spawns a Job that runs helm. That is how CoreDNS, Canal, metrics-server and ingress-nginx get installed — using nothing but ordinary Kubernetes objects.

Until Canal's DaemonSet lands, the node is NotReady with `cni plugin not initialized`. That is expected for the first minute: the network is itself a pod.

code.label: the cluster building itself
code.text:
$ kubectl -n kube-system get helmcharts.helm.cattle.io
NAME                 JOB                             CHART
rke2-canal           helm-install-rke2-canal         rke2-canal
rke2-coredns         helm-install-rke2-coredns       rke2-coredns
rke2-metrics-server  helm-install-rke2-metrics-...   rke2-metrics-server

$ kubectl get nodes
NAME       STATUS   ROLES                       VERSION
server-1   Ready    control-plane,etcd,master   v1.31.4+rke2r1

steps.title: Changing an add-on without losing the change

ask.prompt: You edit the `rke2-coredns` HelmChart object with kubectl. After the next reboot your change is gone. What is the supported way?
choices: A HelmChartConfig with the same name and namespace, in /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests/
Edit the chart values inside the RKE2 binary
Delete the HelmChart and install CoreDNS yourself with helm
Set the values in config.yaml under helm-arg
ask.explain: Anything RKE2 owns in server/manifests/ is regenerated on every start, so direct edits are overwritten. A HelmChartConfig layers your values on top of the chart and survives restarts and upgrades.

steps.body:
This is the single most useful RKE2 habit: never edit what RKE2 generates. Layer on top of it.

The same directory is also a clean way to guarantee your own resources exist before any workload starts — a StorageClass, a PriorityClass, a namespace. RKE2 applies what it finds there, though note it only applies; deleting a file does not remove what it created.

code.label: /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests/rke2-coredns-config.yaml
code.text:
apiVersion: helm.cattle.io/v1
kind: HelmChartConfig
metadata:
  name: rke2-coredns
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  valuesContent: |-
    replicaCount: 3
    resources:
      limits:
        memory: 256Mi

steps.title: Growing etcd, one member at a time

ask.prompt: Why add the second and third servers one at a time rather than starting both together?
choices: Each join changes etcd's membership and quorum requirement; doing them one at a time keeps a healthy majority throughout
Two nodes cannot fetch certificates from the supervisor simultaneously
The token can only be used once at a time
The scheduler would place duplicate static pods
ask.explain: Membership changes are the delicate part of running etcd. Going 1 -> 2 -> 3 keeps a working majority at every moment. It is the same reason you upgrade servers one at a time later.

steps.body:
The additional servers get the same token and the same `tls-san`, plus one extra line: `server: https://k8s-prod.internal:9345`.

On start they contact the **supervisor** on 9345, prove themselves with the token, receive the cluster CAs, join etcd as members, and start their own static pods. Now you have three API servers behind the load balancer and a three-member etcd with a quorum of two.

code.label: config.yaml on server-2 and server-3
code.text:
server: https://k8s-prod.internal:9345
token: <shared-secret>
tls-san:
  - k8s-prod.internal
  - 10.0.0.100
cni: canal
profile: cis

steps.watch: `journalctl -u rke2-server -f` during a join tells you exactly which half failed: a connection refused on 9345 is the network, `failed to validate token` is the secret.

steps.title: An agent is a much smaller thing
steps.body:
A worker runs `rke2-agent` instead of `rke2-server`. Same token, same registration address, but it starts only a kubelet, kube-proxy and containerd. No etcd, no API server, and no `/etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml` — a worker has no admin kubeconfig, by design.

It registers itself with the API server, gets a slice of the pod CIDR, the CNI DaemonSet lands on it, and it goes Ready.

code.label: the finished cluster
code.text:
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME       STATUS   ROLES                       AGE   VERSION
server-1   Ready    control-plane,etcd,master   14m   v1.31.4+rke2r1
server-2   Ready    control-plane,etcd,master   9m    v1.31.4+rke2r1
server-3   Ready    control-plane,etcd,master   6m    v1.31.4+rke2r1
worker-1   Ready    <none>                      2m    v1.31.4+rke2r1

steps.title: The thing that kills quiet clusters

ask.prompt: The cluster has run untouched for 13 months. A server reboots for patching and its API server will not start. Most likely cause?
choices: The one-year certificates expired — RKE2 only rotates them on a restart within 90 days of expiry
etcd lost quorum during the reboot
The containerd socket path changed after the OS update
The token expired
ask.explain: RKE2 issues one-year certificates and rotates them automatically when a server restarts inside the last 90 days. A cluster that never restarts never rotates — so it sails past expiry and dies on the next reboot, which is usually a reboot you did on purpose at a bad moment.

steps.body:
Two maintenance rhythms decide whether this cluster is still healthy in a year:

- **Certificates** — `rke2 certificate check` tells you where you stand. Rotating means stopping the service, `rke2 certificate rotate`, starting it. Put an alert on the expiry date.
- **Snapshots** — taken automatically to `server/db/snapshots/`, but a snapshot on the same disk as etcd is not a backup. Ship them to S3, and test a restore before you need one.

Upgrades follow the same rule as the build: servers first, one at a time, then agents.

code.label: the two commands to schedule
code.text:
$ rke2 certificate check
  serving-kube-apiserver.crt: expires May 02 2027 (243 days)

$ rke2 etcd-snapshot list

# in config.yaml, ship them off the node:
#   etcd-s3: true
#   etcd-s3-bucket: k8s-backups
#   etcd-s3-endpoint: s3.internal

takeaways: The bootstrap works because the kubelet can run static pods from disk with no API server. Everything else follows from that.
config.yaml is the source of truth; RKE2 renders kubelet, containerd and static pod manifests from it. Never edit the generated files.
Port 9345 is registration, 6443 is the API. Set the fixed address and tls-san before the first server ever starts.
Certificates expire after a year and only rotate on restart. A cluster nobody touches is the one that dies on its next reboot.
